Abstract: Voice agents built on large language models (LLMs) now handle customer calls, but in regulated applications completing the task is not enough: the agent must follow a conversational flow set by law. In debt collection, it must confirm it is speaking to the debtor before mentioning the debt, identify itself and the creditor, state the amount, and avoid prohibited language. Every creditor turns these rules into its own procedure and revises it. We ask whether a small, self-hosted policy can be trained once and then follow regulated procedures it has never seen. title: Following the Flow the Law Requires: Training Voice Agents to Transfer to Unseen Regulated Procedures in Debt Collection

Abstract: Under the accelerated pace of AI development, any benchmark whose difficulty is calibrated with humans or current AI systems becomes circular, or saturates soon. How can we then evaluate machines that may become more capable than the current machines and the people who write the tests? One answer to the question hinges on inverse problems, inductive inference questions for which difficulty depends on the complexity of the underlying mechanism, given the observations and the previous knowledge. Levin's Kt, a computable variant of Kolmogorov complexity, puts a theoretical upper bound to that difficulty, balancing the simplest representation encoding for the mechanism and the logarithm of the time steps to run that mechanism. Previous tests derived from Levin's Kt, such as the original C-test, are based on minimalistic Universal Turing Machines (UTM), capable of very limited representations and no previous knowledge. Reasoning large language models (LLM) are UTMs that capture a compendium of human culture as knowledge, using prompts as natural language programs. This paper presents the first test based on Levin's Kt with LLMs as representational machines. Fresh test items can be produced at high difficulties, estimated in a ratio scale measured in bits, before any human or frontier model can solve them. We formalise the measure, devise a lightweight generation and certification pipeline, explore the effect of the power of the reference machine and the gap between examiner and examinee. We produce a first battery of certified items administered to twelve LLMs. The resulting agent characteristic curves decrease with difficulty, down to the uncharted high-difficulty region, the supra-intelligence window of items we can certify, yet beyond generations of frontier intelligence.
title: Artificiality's First Exam: An LLM-Referenced C-test for Supraintelligence

arXiv:2610.14115v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models have significantly lowered the barrier to writing code. Naturally, this has also led to the development of data science agents that promise automating the design and execution of data science from task formulation to model development. Existing evaluations of agentic data science (agentic DS) assess downstream predictive performance and code correctness, providing preliminary insight in agentic DS capabilities. We argue that these evaluations overlook the fundamental principles of data science: methodological data science- and domain knowledge. As such, only assessing downstream performance masks methodological failures such as data leakage and inappropriate validation, limiting the development of robust agentic DS systems. In this paper, we evaluate agentic DS beyond accuracy from three different angles: 1) a large-scale analysis of failure modes in common agentic DS frameworks and models across 220 data science tasks, 2) a reusable and extensible test suite with curated data science tasks that test for six specific failures in a controlled manner, and 3) a qualitative assessment of agentic DS pipelines against expert solutions on Kaggle competitions. We find that the majority of agentic solutions contain at least one failure mode despite the complexity of agentic harness or model capacity. Moreover, we identify a positive correlation between the occurrence of data leakage failures and predictive performance, confirming the necessity to evaluate agents beyond accuracy. Our qualitative analysis shows that DS agents generally lack problem solving creativity and domain knowledge, compared to competition-winning data scientists. We believe that principled failure mode analysis, as presented here, should be integral part of agentic DS evaluations, and that the insights we surface will be key in developing trustworthy agentic DS pipelines.
title: The Silent Failures in Agentic Data Science

arXiv:2610.19026v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sparse attention reduces the KV-cache traffic that dominates long-context LLM decoding, but practical methods largely operate at coarse granularity. Token-level selection offers finer control, yet presents two challenges: low-dimensional scoring may lose query--key structure needed for accurate ranking, while gathering scattered selected tokens can offset the resulting latency benefit. We introduce Joint Subspace Sparse Attention (JSSA) to address both challenges. For selection quality, JSSA learns a shared low-dimensional query--key subspace by minimizing token-score preservation error. We upper-bound the resulting non-convex objective with a tractable marginal objective that admits a closed-form spectral solution; direct refinement of the exact objective provides no measurable improvement in the tested settings. For execution efficiency, we develop a gather-free token-level indexed-attention kernel that supports distinct per-KV-head selections under the standard grouped-query attention (GQA) KV-cache layout. Across standard GQA, hybrid sliding-window/global attention, and Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) models, JSSA consistently remains close to full-KV accuracy while avoiding the substantial generation-length inflation and architecture-dependent failures observed with competing methods. On an NVIDIA B200 GPU, JSSA achieves up to $6.43\times$ the decoding throughput of full-KV attention at 128K context. JSSA achieves reasoning accuracy comparable to model-native DSA without model training and reaches 96--99\% of its decoding throughput even at 700B scale large models.
title: Joint Subspace Sparse Attention for Efficient Long-Context Decoding

Abstract: In so-called "Industry 4.0," integrated sensors, analytics tools, and other digital technologies supplement industrial workflows, potentiating enhanced visibility and automation. Prognostics and health management (PHM) and natural language processing (NLP) practitioners alike have explored the application of large language models (LLMs) to industrial asset management, but many prior works' focus on exam-like benchmarks has limited their assessment of LLMs' ability to automate practical operations. Herein, we introduce CoffeeBench, a fault diagnostics task for LLM agents, using a simulated appliance. The LLMs we evaluate struggle to consistently identify faults from the sensor information alone, but the best-performing ones can iteratively refine the fault-option space to eventually obtain a successful diagnosis. Our subsequent analyses, therefore, focus on: differentiating models by diagnostic efficiency (RQ1); examining the lagging performance of the three worst models (RQ2); and identifying viable heuristics for selective prediction (RQ3), including that initial diagnostic uncertainty and LLM-judged soundness of reasoning are high-signal predictors of diagnostic success. In addition to our benchmark results (Section 3.1), we provide practical insights for improving the performance of the open-weight models on CoffeeBench, such as by explicitly tracking episode state on their behalf to reduce timeouts (Section 3.2) or applying a deliberation loop to refine diagnostic hypotheses (Section 3.3).

We present Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench 2.0 (LHTB 2.0), an extension of Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench that preserves its 46 original tasks while correcting task and evaluation-infrastructure defects and extending 31 tasks. LHTB 2.0 contains 77 tasks across 13 domains and eight task types. The extended tasks are produced through a systematic reconstruction-task pipeline. We start from a working scientific or engineering artifact, then use a parameterized reference implementation to generate multiple scenarios, reveal six as behavioral evidence, hold out three for evaluation, and use dense progress ladders to reward partial progress while preventing memorization of public outputs. We also extend the evaluation horizon from 90 minutes to three hours and record verifier checkpoints every 30 minutes, enabling direct measurement of sustained progress within a run. Across 1,145 scored model-task runs from 15 frontier models, GPT-6-astra leads with dense mean reward 0.69 and 37 tasks at R at least 0.95, followed by GPT-5.6-sol with dense mean reward 0.67 and 32 tasks at the same threshold. On the 30 reconstruction tasks, binary verifier scores average 0.221, whereas dense ladder scores average 0.653, showing that outcome-only evaluation discards substantial intermediate progress. LHTB 2.0 provides a broader, hardened, and process-aware testbed for studying reliable agent execution over hours.
title: Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench 2.0: Automating Diverse Task Construction and Measuring Sustained Agent Progress

arXiv:2610.14180v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Organisations that want language-model agents for security work face a choice between open-weight models, which they can run and audit themselves, and far more expensive closed frontier models. We study that choice on CTI-REALM (arXiv:2603.13517), a benchmark in which an agent turns a threat-intelligence report into a working detection by querying a live telemetry store. We evaluate twenty-six models, nineteen open-weight and seven closed, under a common harness, scorer and panel of LLM judges. Our main finding is that an open-weight model can match the strongest closed models at less than a tenth of their cost, provided it is given enough turns. The benchmark's published limit on agent messages is a confound: a task that exhausts the limit scores zero on every checkpoint, including those it had already passed, so results at that limit partly measure which models finish in time. At the published limit the leading open-weight and closed models cannot be distinguished. With the limit relaxed, the models it was truncating recover, and the highest rewards belong to open-weight models. Among the leading models, price is a poor guide to capability: models with similar rewards differ in cost by more than an order of magnitude. Because the benchmark's checkpoint scores largely record what an agent did or mentioned, we also introduce stage-level metrics that score what the agent submits, by executing its detection queries in the telemetry store and judging its outputs against the answer key. Rather than combining them into one more overall reward, we show that different models lead different stages, which suggests routing each stage of the workflow to the model that performs it best rather than choosing a single model by its overall score. We also report how many tokens each model generates, and find that the share of output spent on thinking does not track the reward.
title: Unconstrained CTI-REALM with Open-Weights

arXiv:2610.14118v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has driven their deployment toward general-purpose harness environments, where LLM-based agents operate in sandbox workspaces and interact directly with file systems and shells. While numerous post-training pipelines exist for tool-use agents, their counterparts for harness-based agents remain scarce and are predominantly one-shot and teacher-dependent: a stronger external model synthesizes tasks and collects trajectories, the target agent is trained once, and evaluation results are consumed by human researchers rather than fed back into the loop. Such pipelines are inherently bounded by the capability of the external model and the scope of human prior, leaving no room for self-improvement. To address these limitations, we propose ClawLoop, a framework that enables self-improving without any external teacher model and with minimal prior dependencies. ClawLoop composes three phases into a self-sustaining cycle: Task Synthesis, which generates a diverse pool of training tasks via two complementary construction routines, applies diagnosis-conditioned difficulty growth followed by both agent-free and agent-based task validation; Training, which updates the agent via SFT and/or RL; and Diagnosis and Feedback, which analyzes the agent's rollout behaviors to produce a capability analysis report that will be used as feedback for task synthesis in the next iteration. Using Qwen3.6-27B as the loop model, ClawLoop yields consistent improvements on SkillsBench, Claw-Eval-Live, and ClawGym-Bench. The iteratively refined tasks are further transferred to smaller-scale Qwen3.5-4B and 9B models with gains across all benchmarks, validating data quality independently of the loop model.
title: ClawLoop: Self-Improving Agents via Harness-Native Training Loop

raw_summary:
In August, we launched the $1M hacker challenge for Vercel Sandbox, inviting security researchers to try and escape Vercel Sandbox. We also coordinated with cybersecurity experts Trail of Bits to review the source code and security architecture.

Here is a summary of the challenge:

  • 1,285 reports over two weeks

  • $242,000 in bounties paid out

  • One Linux kernel zeroday vulnerability uncovered

No reports showed anyone accessing customer data in Vercel Sandbox. The most severe finding was the defect in the upstream Linux kernel.

The kernel zero day

The program's most important report arrived on day three.

Paulos Yibelo (pwn.ai), a HackerOne researcher working from a standard sandbox with no special access, found a defect in the Linux kernel's networking stack. Paulos discovered that specially crafted packets sent from within the microVM enabled three different attacks:

  1. Leak host memory over the network

  2. Crash the host machine

  3. Execute code on the host

Leaking host memory

In the first attack, memory from the host, the machine your sandbox shares with other tenants, shows up in packets the guest sends over the internet. This can happen continuously, for as long as the guest keeps sending.

This attack was demonstrated against Vercel production sandboxes.

Crashing the host and executing code on the host

The researcher also found that by sending specific packets, they could compromise the host.

First, by sending two packets, the researcher crashed the host machine, shutting down every sandbox running on it. Second, using the same flaw, they were able to run commands with full administrator privileges on the host, breaking out of the sandbox’s isolation boundary.

The packet-related crash and code execution attacks were demonstrated on the researcher’s own KVM and Firecracker machines matching Vercel Sandbox configuration.

Responsibly disclosing the kernel vulnerability

Almost every major cloud provider isolates customer workloads on this same layer of the Linux kernel, so any defect is shared-infrastructure risk.

Immediately after being notified, we collaborated with the researcher to understand and mitigate the vulnerability, working with AWS and other industry partners to prioritize a fix, and ensuring that Vercel customers and other developers using the kernel were safe.

The researcher also contacted the kernel maintainers and worked with them to create candidate patches. Fixes are under private review and CVEs are pending, so we are not publishing additional details until the patches are public. We are disclosing the existence of the vulnerability because it was separately disclosed in public.

Our approach to pressure-testing Vercel Sandbox

The HackerOne challenge made bounties available to any researcher, but we also extended our program to include internal evaluations and an independent investigation.

Before launching the public bounty, we performed live security assessments internally with full source access and support from the engineers who created and maintain Vercel Sandbox. We also engaged Trail of Bits, bringing on two engineers to evaluate our security architecture.

Not every finding came from the outside. Marcos Hernanz, a Vercel intern, found a cross-tenant data leak in the Linux device-mapper storage layer. This vulnerability let any sandbox read recycled disk blocks from previously deleted sandboxes.

The white-box deep dive

Trail of Bits spent four engineer-weeks inside our source code, with full access to the repositories and two enterprise test teams. They delivered 20 findings, and each was tested, confirmed, and referenced to the exact code.

They also performed an architectural review and concluded that our virtualization boundary is sound. Each sandbox runs on its own Firecracker microVM with a dedicated guest kernel, and the device model is deliberately tiny. No guest shares a running kernel with the host, or with another tenant.

On top of that foundation, they gave us three structural recommendations, which we implemented:

  • Find and eliminate all trust in the guest. Our control plane accepted values returned by software running inside the microVM, and every one of those values is tenant input. Anything that crosses the boundary should be derived server-side or signed with a key the guest cannot reach.

  • One policy, one decider. Egress enforcement was split across subsystems that each parsed the same network policy independently, and they did not always agree. We now use one canonicalization routine per data type, one component per decision, and revalidate connections when policy changes.

  • Assume the next zero day. We strengthened the protections around each sandbox to limit the damage if an attacker exploits the virtualization software. We keep host kernels up to date, have disabled nested virtualization, and use Firecracker’s jailer to run each microVM process with restricted permissions and isolate it from the rest of the host.

Vercel Sandbox findings

We received 1,285 reports in two weeks. This volume is only possible because researchers now hunt at AI speed.

Here is a breakdown of reports by category:

  • 877 duplicates

  • 319 not applicable

  • 57 valid

  • 32 informative

In our report triage we have validated:

  • 1 Critical finding

  • 5 High findings

  • 9 Medium findings

  • 42 Low findings

  • 32 Informative findings

We have paid out $242,000 in bug bounties.

The medium, Low, and Informative findings are small policy-boundary gaps, like a firewall rule that behaved differently than documented and a field that trusted the guest more than it should.

The most severe finding was the Linux kernel zero day defect, and no reports showed anyone reading a customer’s files, secrets, or application data.

We were most impressed with the heterogeneity of the reports. It was clear that researchers used different setups and have different obsessions. Some clearly know Linux namespaces and steered their agents straight at the kernel boundary. Others went after the network policies, and many went after areas we didn’t think to put on the menu.

That variety is what you're funding with a public challenge. Here's one of the more interesting findings it produced.

Cross-tenant disk snapshot restore (with limits)

Filed on day one of the challenge, this report is our favorite example of why we run a public bug bounty, even after internal assessments and a white-box engagement.

When you snapshot a sandbox, the control plane has to record where the snapshot data landed: {storage_url, size, checksum}. The flaw the researcher found was subtle: that answer came from software running inside the guest, and services running on the host trusted it. That is a trust-boundary violation. The guest is where our customers (and hackers) run untrusted code, so the host can never take its word as authoritative.

The researcher combined a known, documented container-escape primitive with this trust flaw. They intercepted the snapshot response inside their own sandbox and rewrote it, swapping the storage objects of two snapshots belonging to two separate accounts they owned. That meant restoring "your" snapshot materialized the other account's entire filesystem.

The researcher demonstrated that each account could read and modify the other’s files, verified the results using hashes, and preserved the test resources so we could independently reproduce the findings.

The limits of this attack matter. Aiming the swap at a specific victim required knowing that victim's internal snapshot storage key, a random 96-bit identifier the platform generates per snapshot and never exposes through the API. The only place that key appears is inside the victim's own sandbox. The researcher owned both accounts, which is what made the proof possible; there was no demonstrated path for a stranger to target another tenant. We still treated it as a priority fix, because a boundary that depends on a secret staying secret is not a boundary.

Trail of Bits independently flagged the same root cause in their assessment, which told us the finding was real, important, and discoverable from two completely different angles.

The fix shipped within a week, and the control plane now binds every snapshot object to the project that created it and rejects anything else. Snapshot creation moved out of the guest-reachable environment into a host-side service, and storage paths are project-scoped with strictly validated URLs.

Thank you to the research community

We would like to thank every researcher who filed a report, whether their finding was a zero day or a duplicate. Every technique discovered in the challenge informs how we protect the workloads running on Vercel Sandbox.

Thank you also to Trail of Bits for your comprehensive internal investigation and guidance.

Read the original challenge announcement and learn more about Vercel Sandbox in the documentation.

analysis.summary_cn: The generative AI functions in BigQuery (AI.GENERATE, AI.IF, AI.CLASSIFY, AI.SCORE, and more) bring large language models (LLMs) directly into your SQ

raw_summary:
The generative AI functions in BigQuery (AI.GENERATE, AI.IF, AI.CLASSIFY, AI.SCORE, and more) bring large language models (LLMs) directly into your SQL, so a single query can classify millions of support tickets or score each product review for sentiment. However, because these functions are billed by the token, scaling them across massive datasets highlights the importance of managing your budget proactively. 

We recently announced the general availability (GA) of token-based cost management for BigQuery generative AI functions: daily quotas that let administrators set self-serve guardrails on AI token consumption, so teams can innovate while staying within your budget. In this blog, we provide an overview of cost management for BigQuery generative AI functions, walk through a few practical examples, and share resources to help you get started. Let’s jump in.  

Quotas for managing costs

Four daily quotas, managed through the Google Cloud Identity and Access Management (IAM) quota system, provide controls at the project level and the per-user level. Per-user limits apply to each user within a project, not across your organization.

Key details:

  • The quotas are global. Usage is summed across all regions, so costs can't pile up unnoticed in a region you weren't watching.

  • Output quotas include "thinking" tokens. Reasoning tokens count toward your output quota, just as they count toward your Gemini platform bill.

Which functions are covered?

The quotas apply to these BigQuery functions that perform LLM-backed generation:

  • AI.GENERATE

  • AI.GENERATE_TABLE

  • AI.GENERATE_TEXT (and its alias ML.GENERATE_TEXT)

  • AI.CLASSIFY

  • AI.IF

  • AI.SCORE

  • AI.AGG

What's not covered: Embedding functions such as AI.GENERATE_EMBEDDING (also available as ML.GENERATE_EMBEDDING) and AI.EMBED are not subject to these quotas, because they run on different, substantially cheaper models.

Managing your quotas

Administrators can view and adjust the quotas directly in the Google Cloud console as workloads change, with no support case required.

  1. Navigate to IAM & Admin → Quotas & System Limits.

  2. Filter by service and select BigQuery API.

  3. Sort by the Name column to bring the four AI quotas to the top.

4. Find the quota, for example AI input tokens per day.

5. Open the three-dot menu and choose Edit quota.

From there:

  • To tighten cost control, lower a quota. This takes effect immediately with no approval needed.

  • To support higher usage, request an increase from the same page. Many requests are auto-approved; larger increases may go through a quick review.

You'll need the right permissions. You need one of: Owner, Editor, Quota Administrator (roles/servicemanagement.quotaAdmin), or Service Usage Admin (roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageAdmin).

Prefer automation? You can also manage these quotas programmatically through the Cloud Quotas API, the gcloud CLI, and Terraform to apply consistent guardrails across projects.

Monitoring usage

Beyond setting limits, the Quotas & System Limits page displays your historical token consumption so you can quickly detect spikes and right-size your budgets. Use these trends to see how new generative AI workloads and data pipelines affect your overall token usage.

For a step-by-step walkthrough, see the BigQuery documentation on controlling costs with token quotas.

Token quotas vs. billing spend caps

Token quotas aren't the only cost guardrail in Google Cloud.

  • Token quotas (this feature) are preventive and AI-specific. BigQuery tracks token usage during query execution and stops work close to the limit, with separate limits per project and per user.

  • Cloud Billing spend caps operate on dollars at the project and service level and can automatically block usage when a threshold is reached. They're a broad, financial backstop rather than a precise usage control, and because enforcement is not instant, some overages are incurred.

Use token quotas as your first line of defense for AI spend, and a spend cap as a project-wide safety net.

How enforcement works

Quotas are enforced by stopping work rather than letting a query run past your limit. A query is rejected up front with a QuotaExceeded error only if a quota it needs is already exhausted. Otherwise, it starts, and if a quota runs out mid-query, BigQuery stops sending new LLM calls:

  • Functions that support max_error_ratio (such as AI.IF) return partial results if unprocessed rows stay within the ratio, and otherwise fail.

  • General-purpose functions (such as AI.GENERATE) still succeed. Skipped rows have no generated value, and their status field contains the quota-exceeded error.

For details, see quota enforcement behavior in the documentation.

Sizing your input data: AI.COUNT_TOKENS

To choose quota values, it helps to know how much text your workloads send to a model. The AI.COUNT_TOKENS function helps with this.

AI.COUNT_TOKENS returns the number of tokens a model's tokenizer produces for a text string, without making a billable generation call. Run it over a column to measure your input data:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "-- Count the input text tokens for each product review\r\nSELECT\r\n SUM(\r\n AI.COUNT_TOKENS(\r\n CONCAT('Classify the sentiment of this review as positive, negative, or neutral: ', review_text),\r\n\r\n endpoint => 'gemini-3.1-flash-lite').result) AS total_input_tokens\r\nFROM\r\n `my_project.my_dataset.product_reviews`;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fc0a527b950>)])]>

The count is a lower bound on input tokens. It doesn't include output or thinking tokens, the instructions each AI function adds around your input, or non-text inputs such as images. Use it to:

  • Gauge the input side of a workload before you launch it.

  • Right-size your quotas together with a small sample run that measures actual input and output usage.

  • Translate tokens into dollars using the published Gemini platform pricing for your model.

From tokens to budget: a worked example

Suppose you want to keep a project's daily AI spend around $100 with the Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite model. As of today's published pricing (BigQuery processes in batch which provides a 50% discount):

  • Input tokens: $0.125 per 1 million tokens

  • Output tokens (response + reasoning): $0.75 per 1 million tokens

If a small sample run shows an average 100:1 input-to-output token ratio, you can solve for a daily budget:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Cost: 0.125 × I + 0.75 × O = 100 (I, O in millions of tokens)\r\nRatio: I = 100 × O'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fc0a5579650>)])]>

Solving gives about 754 million input tokens and 7.54 million output tokens per day. Set AI input tokens per day and AI output tokens per day to these values to hold the project near $100/day. If a project uses models with different prices, budget per model or blend the rates.

Best practices for managing AI cost

  • Start with per-user quotas. They stop one user or runaway experiment from draining the project's budget.

  • Measure before you scale. Use AI.COUNT_TOKENS to size your input, then check a small sample run in the usage chart before setting limits.

  • Mind the output side. Output tokens cost more. Where a function accepts max_output_tokens, set it to bound generation length.

  • Monitor and iterate. Adjust limits as real usage and budgets change.

Get started

Token-based cost management is available now. To begin:

  1. Open IAM & Admin → Quotas & System Limits in the Google Cloud Console and filter by BigQuery API.

  2. Review the four AI-related token quotas and set limits that match your budget.

  3. Use AI.COUNT_TOKENS to size your input data.

For the full details, see the documentation on controlling generative AI costs.

With token-based guardrails in place, your teams can use generative AI in BigQuery with the cost predictability your organization needs.

arXiv:2610.19134v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Feature distillation is usually expected to add to logit distillation. We find that this expectation does not hold for two common feature losses in compact multilingual automatic speech recognition (ASR), and analyze why through their gradients. The gradient of a projection-based loss is orthogonal to the task gradient, while that of Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA), a similarity-based loss, is weakly aligned with it. CKA lowers the word error rate (WER) on non-English languages, but at the expense of data-rich English. Three loss-level remedies (one trained, two probed) all fall short, and the CKA gradient overlaps with the subspace English uses in the shared encoder by 97.5% to 99.5% (about 81% by chance). Guided by this diagnosis, we propose CAFE (Confined-Adapter Feature distillation), which confines the CKA gradient to adapters that English bypasses, addressing the trade-off in the parameters rather than in the loss. On the Open ASR Leaderboard, CAFE lowers the average WER from 8.55% to 8.02%, beats an adapter-only capacity control at 8.51%, and makes English more stable across checkpoints. At 254M parameters, it trails the 0.6B teacher by 2 WER points and is competitive with much larger models across 48 test sets in 24 languages. We use 564k hours of training data and state-of-the-art models to keep the findings relevant to practice.

AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary.

Indie game developer Popcar talks about the recent wave of AI-powered decompilation of existing games, enabling weird mashups between existing games, and producing a boom in game preservation projects to get old games working on new hardware (often in a browser using WebAssembly).

I like how this piece captures both the positives and the negatives of this new development:

Most people already realized the scary part by now. If AI can decompile games and software, then the entire tech industry is about to explode. Anybody can decompile other software and use it any way they'd like, and nobody can stop them. Companies can steal from competitors. Your paid game or app can be open-sourced against your will. This isn't exclusive to old video games, we can apply this to any software. [...]

This is also a big win for preservation. Old games can be ported, modified, enhanced, and made much more easily accessible than before. [...[

With console makers going all in on digital and games becoming entirely unplayable due to servers shutting down, this is fantastic news. We could own software we bought regardless of what the company thinks.

Via Hacker News

raw_summary:
arXiv:2610.19206v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While work on LLM-based regression has largely focused on scalar prediction, multi-output text regression remains less explored. We present DualView, a parameter-efficient approach to leverage LLMs for multi-output text regression. \method{} first extracts broad and output-specific representations from a frozen LLM, then uses a dual-branch architecture to produce the full score vector. Across five heterogeneous regression tasks and eight LLMs (up to 122B), DualView outperforms seven supervised regression baselines while requiring 82--1842 times fewer fitted parameters than the three strongest baselines. These improvements extend across individual output dimensions and persist even with limited training data. Notably, DualView using a smaller open-weight LLM can outperform unsupervised prediction with Gemini 3.1 Pro. Controlled ablations show that broad and output-specific evidence provide complementary predictive benefits, while lightweight shared predictors achieve strong performance with fewer trainable parameters.
title: DUALVIEW: Leveraging Broad and Output-Specific Evidence for LLM-based Multi-Output Text Regression

analysis.summary_cn: 该研究提出 Parallel-Then-Integrated（PTI）四步流程，用于整合同一质性语料的两种计算表示，提升混合方法研究的可追踪性。作者以尼泊尔 29 位母亲的 1203 段访谈为案例，将本体引导的 Patient Voice 编码（PVminer）与 NMF 数据驱动主题做主题完备的交叉映射，并用 PHQ-9 抑郁状态作外部锚点进行探索性关联检验。

raw_summary:
arXiv:2610.19164v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mixed methods research offers established strategies for integrating qualitative and quantitative evidence, but less guidance for integrating two computational representations of the same qualitative corpus. This methodological study introduces Parallel-Then-Integrated (PTI), a four-step procedure for explicit and traceable integration. We present PTI using 1,203 interview paragraphs from 29 mothers in Nepal. The two representations were ontology-guided Patient Voice (PV) coding with PVminer and data-driven themes generated through non-negative matrix factorization (NMF). A theme-complete crosswalk documented convergence, divergence, and preprocessing-sensitive differences. Depression status, based on Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) scores, served as a secondary external anchor for exploratory association checks. PTI provides a structured approach for integrating computational representations of qualitative text within mixed methods research.
title: From Qualitative Text to Integrated Evidence: The Parallel-Then-Integrated (PTI) Procedure
